Deutsches Historisches Museum's account of the Warsaw Genuflection (1970)

risk_tolerance.rationale: Two independent, extremely high-stakes documented instances: became one of the first to openly resist Hitler's regime immediately after its January 1933 rise, adopting an assumed identity for protection and going into exile in Norway, where sustained anti-Nazi political activity led directly to his German citizenship being revoked (1938); and fled a second country, Sweden, in 1940 under direct German occupation threat.

independent_thinking.rationale: Pursued Ostpolitik (reconciliation with Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union) as a deliberate, sustained policy position directly against the dominant Cold War-era West German political consensus, sustaining the policy through years of severe domestic political attack (labeled a "Verzichtspolitiker," or renunciation politician, by opponents).

conflict_tolerance.rationale: Sustained Ostpolitik through years of vocal, organized domestic political opposition that accused him of a "sell-out of German interests," rather than moderating the policy, ultimately winning a landslide re-election in late 1972 on the same platform.

proactive_agency.rationale: His 1970 kneeling gesture before the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising memorial during a state visit to Poland is specifically documented as unplanned and spontaneous, not a scripted diplomatic protocol item, remaining silently in that position for roughly 30 seconds -- a genuinely self-initiated, in-the-moment act beyond any formal diplomatic requirement.

decisiveness.rationale: When a top aide, Gunter Guillaume, was revealed to be an East German intelligence agent (April 1974), Brandt personally assumed political responsibility and resigned as Chancellor within roughly two weeks (May 6, 1974), rather than deflecting blame or delaying a decision.

leadership_drive.rationale: Served as Chancellor of West Germany (1969-1974) and, even after resigning that role over the Guillaume affair, continued leading the Social Democratic Party as its chairman for a further thirteen years (until 1987) -- sustained institutional leadership across two distinct formal capacities over decades.
